q: What is the most common cause of non-traumatic subarachnoid haemorrhage?
why: About 85% of SAH is aneurysmal, 10% AVM.

q: A patient with a thunderclap headache has a normal CT. What test is next if suspicion remains?
o: Lumbar puncture after 12 hours looking for xanthochromia
why: Xanthochromia (red cell breakdown) takes about 12 hours to develop.

q: What nimodipine regimen is used after SAH?
why: Nimodipine 60 mg 4-hourly for 21 days reduces delayed cerebral ischaemia.

q: When is vasospasm most likely after SAH?
why: Delayed cerebral ischaemia and vasospasm occur from around day 3–14; rebleeding and hydrocephalus are early complications.

q: During coiling under GA, the aneurysm ruptures with a sudden rise in BP and fall in heart rate. What should you prepare?
o: Protamine to reverse heparin, BP control and EVD drainage
why: Reverse heparin with protamine, control BP, drain the EVD and support CPP.

q: What heparin target is used during neurointerventional coiling?
why: Heparin 70–100 u/kg aiming for ACT 2–3× baseline.

q: A patient with SAH has T-wave inversion and a raised troponin. What is the likely explanation?
o: Neurogenic stunned myocardium from catecholamine surge
why: SAH can stun the myocardium (neurogenic), with ECG changes, raised troponin and pulmonary oedema.

q: Which aneurysm location is most common?
why: ACOM about 40%, MCA about 34%, PCOM about 20%.

q: Which clinical sign suggests a posterior communicating artery aneurysm?
o: Isolated third nerve palsy with a dilated pupil
why: A PCOM aneurysm compresses CN III, causing a dilated pupil.

q: What is an advantage of coiling over surgical clipping?
o: Less invasive and better for posterior circulation aneurysms
why: Coiling is less invasive and suits posterior circulation aneurysms; clipping has a lower recurrence rate and treats all types.
